title: Classes
summary: A class describes how to make objects with the same kinds of values and actions.
introduction: A class describes how to make objects with the same kinds of values and actions. Make a simple class, then label its properties and methods. A property stores a value; a method is an action the object can do.
learningObjectives: Declare typed fields, constructors and methods and fix strict property initialisation errors
Apply public, private, protected and readonly, including the parameter-property shorthand
Use abstract classes, implements and override to build small hierarchies safely

blocks.text: Fields are declared with a type above the constructor, assigned inside it, and used by methods through `this`. Method parameters and return types are annotated exactly like standalone functions, and calls on an instance are checked the same way.

blocks.title: account.ts
npx tsc account.ts
blocks.content:
account.ts:19:17 - error TS2345: Argument of type 'string' is not assignable to parameter of type 'number'.

19 account.deposit("50");
                   ~~~~


Found 1 error in account.ts:19

blocks.text: Up to the last line the program prints `Ada: 150`. In JavaScript, `deposit("50")` would turn the balance into the string `"15050"` through concatenation; a bug that the type on `amount` makes impossible.

Under `strict`, the `strictPropertyInitialization` check requires every field to receive a value in its declaration or in the constructor. A field that is assigned later in a method is reported, because until that method runs the field is `undefined` while its type says `number`.

blocks.title: timer.ts
npx tsc timer.ts
blocks.content:
timer.ts:2:3 - error TS2564: Property 'startedAt' has no initializer and is not definitely assigned in the constructor.

2   startedAt: number;
    ~~~~~~~~~


Found 1 error in timer.ts:2

blocks.text: Three honest fixes: give the field a default (`startedAt = 0`), make the type admit the missing state (`startedAt: number | undefined`, or `startedAt?: number`), or assign it in the constructor. The dishonest fix is `startedAt!: number`, the *definite assignment assertion*, which tells the compiler to trust you; use it only when a framework guarantees the assignment before any method runs.

`public` (the default), `private` and `protected` control who may access a member: anyone, only the class itself, or the class and its subclasses. `readonly` allows assignment only in the declaration or constructor. Putting a modifier on a constructor parameter, a *parameter property*, declares the field and assigns it in one step. JavaScript's own `#name` syntax declares a field that is private at runtime as well.

blocks.title: counter.ts
npx tsc counter.ts
blocks.content:
counter.ts:15:21 - error TS2341: Property 'step' is private and only accessible within class 'Counter'.

15 console.log(counter.step);
                       ~~~~


Found 1 error in counter.ts:15

blocks.text: The first `console.log` prints `2 4 counter`. The constructor body is empty because the two parameter properties do all the work. Parameter properties are convenient but, like enums, they are not erasable syntax: Node's type stripping and `erasableSyntaxOnly` reject them, so projects that depend on type stripping write the fields out by hand.

blocks.title: Common mistake: thinking private hides data
blocks.text: TypeScript's `private` is checked at compile time only. The emitted JavaScript has an ordinary property: `(counter as any).step` reads it, `Object.keys(counter)` lists it and `JSON.stringify` serialises it. If a value must be unreachable from outside, use a `#private` field, which the JavaScript engine enforces and which never shows up in `Object.keys`. Use TypeScript's `private` for API design, not for security.

`implements` checks that a class satisfies an interface. An `abstract` class cannot be instantiated and may declare `abstract` methods that subclasses must provide. `override` marks a method that replaces a base-class method; the compiler then reports a typo in the method name instead of silently creating a second, unrelated method. With `noImplicitOverride` on, the keyword becomes mandatory.

blocks.title: shapes.ts

blocks.text: `shapes` is typed as `Shape[]`, an array of the interface, so the loop can only call `area()`; `describe()` belongs to `BaseShape`, not to the interface. Structural typing applies to classes too: any object with an `area(): number` method would satisfy `Shape`, whether or not it came from this hierarchy.

rows: Compile-time access control: everyone, the class only, the class and subclasses
Runtime-private field enforced by JavaScript; not visible to `Object.keys` or `JSON.stringify`
Assignable only in the declaration or the constructor
Belongs to the class, not to instances (`Temperature.fromFahrenheit(98.6)`)
Class cannot be instantiated; abstract members must be implemented by subclasses
Declares that a method replaces an inherited one; a misspelled name becomes an error

blocks.title: Classes are optional
blocks.text: Much TypeScript code uses plain objects, interfaces and functions instead of classes. Reach for a class when you need encapsulated state with behaviour, when a framework such as [Angular](/tutorials/angular) expects one, or when `instanceof` checks are useful. The [narrowing lesson](/tutorials/typescript/narrowing) shows `instanceof` as a type guard.

questions.question: What does `constructor(private readonly id: number) {}` do?
questions.explanation: A modifier on a constructor parameter turns it into a parameter property: the field is declared with that type and visibility and assigned from the argument automatically.
options: Declares a local variable `id` that only the constructor can use
Declares a private, read-only field `id` and assigns the argument to it
Makes the constructor private so the class cannot be instantiated
Creates a static property shared by all instances

questions.question: A class marked `abstract` can still be instantiated with `new` as long as it has no abstract methods.
questions.explanation: The abstract keyword on the class itself forbids new, regardless of its members. Only concrete subclasses can be instantiated.
